# Confluence Complete Game Design

Confluence is a 3D first person magical fantasy game for PC. Players master a wizard whose casting method changes how they prepare and execute spells, build a loadout through shared equipment purchases and free augment drafts, and fight individual opponents in arenas that change every round. The complete game contains 36 wizards, 288 wizard exclusive spells, 120 shared equipment definitions, 864 free augmentations, 24 arena biomes, 72 terrain modules, 48 interactive prop definitions, and 48 worked build examples.

The central promise is that a player can win through execution, movement, preparation, or the inventive use of shared physical rules. Precision matters, but the arena can also become a shield, an approach route, a trap, a conductor, or a resource to deny. This document specifies the complete end state and concrete initial tuning values. Balance and performance figures are design targets to verify in production, rather than claims of completed playtesting.

## 1 Game identity and scope

### Experience pillars

- Distinct casting. Choosing a wizard changes the act of casting, its cadence, its opportunities, and its vulnerabilities. A wizard's grammar remains recognizable when they equip different schools of magic.
- Interactive battlefields. Players understand and deliberately manipulate heat, water, ice, cover, force, conductivity, visibility, and sound. Important reactions have consistent rules and visible causes.
- Complete melee and ranged combat. Closing distance, holding distance, defending, repositioning, and punishing recovery are all supported. Every valid arena offers routes and engagements for both styles.
- Run based construction. Choices made between fights develop a build over one match. Money for shared equipment, six equipped exclusive spell slots, and six free augmentation choices constrain the build without reducing its possible combinations.
- Earned mastery. Difficult inputs earn control or efficiency under pressure. A reliable normal cast remains available; complicated controls alone do not award superior baseline power.
- Readable competition. An opponent can identify the cause of a major attack, see a defensive opening, and understand why they lost. Cosmetic effects cannot obscure the relevant information.

The view stays first person during active combat. Third person appears only in the lobby, fitting room, spectator camera, and replay. The main platform is Windows PC with mouse and keyboard as the default input. Controller input is supported through full remapping and analogue substitutes, without competitive aim assistance. Casting alternatives are selectable before matchmaking and visible on the training screen; the opponent sees the same commitment and telegraph.

The visual world is grounded fantasy with physically convincing materials, readable silhouettes, and stylized magical effects. The game depicts spell impacts, armor damage, and magical dissipation without requiring graphic bodily injury. There is no persistent statistical progression, paid power, or premium reroll currency.

Confluence is a fictional working title for this design. The game world is the Conclave, a network of floating duel grounds rebuilt from fragments of a fractured magical continent. Matches are authorized contests, and defeated wizards are recalled through their oathmarks. This explains repeated fights, changing arenas, restoration between rounds, and spectral spectators without making every combat result a story death.

### Player goals

Within a fight, defeat the opponent or finish the timer with the greater fraction of health. Within a Conclave match, preserve Resolve and become the final surviving contender. Across matches, improve casting mastery, discover builds, complete non-power collections, and climb the competitive ladder.

There are no mandatory daily tasks or grind requirements to access wizards, spells, gear, or upgrades. All gameplay definitions are available on account creation. The codex teaches their use; it does not unlock statistical advantages.

## 2 Complete match structure

### Main mode Conclave

Eight solo players enter one lobby. A player selects one wizard for the entire match. Every round pairs the remaining players into simultaneous 1v1 fights. Each pair occupies a separate copy of the same generated round arena, so terrain, diameter, weather gameplay state, and prop placement are identical across pairs. The seed changes between rounds. Builds, individual interactions, and destruction evolve independently inside each copy.

Every player starts with 8 Resolve. Resolve is match survival, separate from the 300 point health pool restored for each duel. Losing a duel removes 1 Resolve in rounds 1 through 3, 2 in rounds 4 through 6, 3 in rounds 7 through 9, and 4 in rounds 10 through 12. Reaching zero eliminates the player after the current simultaneous round finishes. A draw removes the scheduled loss amount from both players and gives neither a winner bonus. Resolve cannot be purchased, healed, or stolen.

The regular schedule ends early when one contender remains. After round 12, any remaining contenders enter a seeded single elimination bracket with a maximum of three bracket rounds. Seeds use Resolve, combat wins, fewer byes, and finally a recorded lobby seed for exact ties. Highest seeds receive bracket byes needed to reach a power of two. Every bracket loss eliminates its loser, irrespective of remaining Resolve. Currency and loadouts continue through bracket rounds; tier 4 stays unlocked. A bracket draw replays once with the same loadouts, full resources, no shop, and a new balanced arena seed. A second draw records a shared finish occupying the mean of the tied placement positions. It does not grant a sole champion badge.

Eliminated players can leave immediately without a penalty. They may instead spectate, inspect builds, practice in a separate lobby target space, or watch replays. These actions cannot communicate hidden information to live players through game channels. Placements among players eliminated during the same regular round are tied; rewards use the mean of the occupied placement positions rather than an arbitrary damage statistic.

### Round sequence

1. Reveal the next opponent and generated arena. Show diameter, biome, major terrain, props, and remaining Resolve. Reveal the opponent's completed previous-round loadout; live purchases remain hidden until combat starts.
2. Open the shop for 35 seconds. Players receive scheduled income, purchase shared equipment from three offers, reroll individual equipment cards, sell eligible equipment, and set six spells from their wizard’s eight-spell kit. On an augment round, a separate 30 second free five-choice draft follows this phase. A player can ready early; the next phase begins early only if every active player is ready.
3. Place both players in protected spawn alcoves for 5 seconds. Restore health, mana, stamina, cooldowns, consumables owned for the round, and signature resources. The ward prevents damage and casting; players may look, move within the alcove, and inspect their loadout. Opponent final loadouts become visible.
4. Open the alcoves and begin combat. No opponent is visible from the exact initial spawn position. The round lasts at most 90 seconds.
5. At 55 seconds the boundary begins its announced contraction. It reaches the validated central 8 meter duel space at 85 seconds. It follows a path that never cuts off every usable route from an occupied region.
6. Resolve the duel on death, surrender, or time. Allow an 8 second results period while the other arenas finish. Show health, major interactions, damage channels, and winner. Fast winners can spectate other pairs through delayed information.

Boundary damage is 15 health per second for the first 2 seconds outside, then 30 per second, then 60 per second after 4 seconds. It bypasses shields, resistance, guard, healing reduction, and invulnerability-like effects. It is a match rule and cannot trigger any item or augmentation. Returning inside resets the escalation after 1 second. Teleports cannot end outside the legal boundary. Forced displacement stops at its edge with a small 5 point impact rather than ejecting someone into unavoidable boundary damage.

At the 90 second timer, compare current health divided by that player's maximum health, excluding shields and temporary borrowed health. A difference below 0.5 percentage points is a draw. Otherwise the greater fraction wins. This judgement is shown throughout the final 15 seconds as a small equal, ahead, or behind indicator. Simultaneous lethal outcomes within the same authoritative simulation step are draws. A surrender is a normal loss and cannot avoid Resolve loss.

Typical matches target 14 to 24 minutes. A full 12 round schedule, six 30 second augment drafts, and three bracket rounds can approach 39 minutes; draw replays add at most a few further minutes. The UI states the expected duration before queuing. A reconnect is allowed for 90 seconds; an absent player can lose rounds normally, and disconnecting never pauses an opponent's duel.

### Pairing and byes

Regular pairing minimizes a cost over all possible pairings: immediate rematches are the largest cost, repeating any of the previous two opponents is next, and Resolve difference then combat-win difference determine the preferred remaining pairs. The server evaluates the complete small pairing set rather than greedily pairing the first players. Exact cost ties use the recorded round seed. Spawn side alternates when possible, with no player receiving the same side more than twice consecutively when a legal alternative exists.

If there is an odd survivor count, the bye goes to the player with the fewest previous regular byes, then the player who has waited longest since a bye, then a seeded tie. A bye preserves Resolve, awards normal baseline income, and gives no combat win and no 100 Crown winner bonus. Bye players may shop and practice in the lobby range; the practice session cannot generate resources, cooldown progress, or information used in combat. The bracket uses its own explicitly seeded bye rule.

### Additional complete modes

- Duel. Two players play a best of seven with the same round economy and tier schedule. Tiers unlock in duel rounds 1, 2, 4, and 6 so the build reaches late-game variety. A tied duel replays the round with the same loadouts and no extra income. After two replays it scores one half win each, advancing the round number; at a 3.5 to 3.5 finish, one deciding round is played. Two drawn deciders produce a recorded match draw. A private rematch can reuse wizard choices or reset them.
- Unranked Conclave. The complete main rules without ladder impact. Matchmaking still considers skill, connection, and party restrictions. Solo players cannot enter ranked Conclave as a coordinated group.
- Ranked Conclave. Eight solo players, fixed competition rules, all gameplay content available, and placement rating. This is the primary public ranked queue.
- Ranked Duel. A separate 1v1 rating with the Duel rules. Queue health is monitored separately; the UI estimates wait times rather than silently mixing ladders.
- Laboratory. A solo or invited partner sandbox with any catalogue content, editable mana, cooldown, damage, gravity, reaction budgets, and saved arena seeds. Modified sessions are clearly labeled and have no ranked rewards.
- Trials. Authored aim, gesture, voice, rhythm, movement, parry, reaction, and build-planning challenges. Leaderboards separate input methods when the measured task depends on input hardware.
- Custom Conclave. Hosts configure player count 2 through 8, rule presets, seed rotation, shop timer, starting Crowns, allowed catalogue entries, and spectator delay. A settings fingerprint is visible before joining. Custom rules never appear as standard ranked results.
- Versus constructs. Solo Duel or Conclave against bots with adjustable competence. Bots obey resource, cast, vision, and reaction rules and do not read hidden player inputs. A training-only telegraph predictor can be enabled openly.

## 3 Core combat and controls

### Common numerical foundation

All wizards begin every duel with 300 health, 100 mana, and 100 stamina. Base health, mana, and stamina do not increase with round number. Bought effects produce all progression. No player has passive health regeneration. Mana regenerates at 10 per second after 1.5 seconds without spending mana; stamina regenerates at 20 per second after 1 second without spending stamina. Channels continuously count as spending. Mana regeneration is capped at 14 per second after modifiers. A player cannot cast without enough resource to pay the full initial commitment.

Walk speed is 5.5 meters per second and sprint speed is 7 meters per second. Sprint costs 12 stamina per second, disallows channeled beams and normal melee strikes, and remains compatible with selected quick casts at their declared movement penalties. A normal jump costs 10 stamina. Air steering is moderate and cannot reverse horizontal momentum immediately. There is no universal double jump, bunny-hop acceleration, or slide speed stacking. Effects that add jumps or wall movement specify resource and duration, and respect the movement caps.

Dodge costs 25 stamina, travels 3 meters over 0.22 seconds, and has a 1.6 second cooldown. It provides movement without invulnerability. Jumping, dodging, and sprinting are equally available to every wizard. A mastered movement input changes its stated utility rather than granting unexplained avoidance frames.

Default inputs are movement on WASD, aim on mouse, cast on primary mouse button, guard on secondary mouse button, sprint on Shift, jump on Space, crouch on Ctrl, dodge on Alt, selected spell slots on 1 through 6 or wheel, common melee on F, signature on Q, active equipment on E, consumable on X, spell recast on T, and cast modifier on R. Modifier A and Modifier B default to Z and C. Every binding is remappable, and conflicts are detected before a ranked queue. Holding a spell-selection wheel slows neither opponent nor game time.

The wizard grammar acts on the selected spell. A reliable normal cast always follows that spell's windup. Optional mastery input adds the wizard's stated preparation, exposure, and reward; it cannot remove an unavoidable spell windup. If a grammar temporarily uses mouse movement, the player explicitly holds its modifier to enter that mode, sees a camera-lock cue, and can cancel immediately. Aim resumes at the held view, without unannounced camera snapping. Spell selection and signature input never require opening a menu during combat.

### Casting phases and interruption

Every cast has preparation, commitment, release, and recovery. Before commitment, cancellation spends no mana but preserves any elapsed exposed preparation and gives a 0.15 second re-cast lock. At commitment, mana is paid and cooldown begins. Interrupting a committed cast spends its resource and starts the normal cooldown; the player receives a 25 percent mana refund only if the spell explicitly has the universal interrupt-refund tag. Voluntary cancellation after commitment gives no refund. No refund effect may exceed 25 percent of the original paid resource or fire more than once per cast.

Cast time in a spell record is the windup before release. Instant means zero windup, not zero recovery. Quick projectiles use 0.20 seconds recovery, heavy projectiles and control spells 0.35, and major fields or summons 0.45 unless a record states a longer recovery. Channeled effects can be cancelled on any simulation step; their remaining ticks stop. Maximum normal channel duration is 3 seconds. Movement while casting is 70 percent of walk speed for heavy/control/field casts and 85 percent for quick casts; a stationary requirement overrides this explicitly. A signature cannot hide those phases.

Spell recast acts only on the selected spell’s currently pending recast state and does nothing when none exists. It never silently starts a new spell. A recast uses the original paid cast’s event identity and mastery result; unless its record states a further resource payment, it has no additional mana cost and grants no paid-cast refund, rotation credit, or second on-cast trigger. Its allowed window, number of recasts, visible telegraph, and added recovery come from the exact spell or augment. A missing recast window defaults to once during the original effect’s remaining lifetime, never after that effect has ended.

Visible hand pose, focus animation, ground marks, projectile shapes, and audio communicate stages. A threat above 70 direct damage, a hard-control spell, and a teleport destination always have a minimum 0.25 second anticipatory cue, even when the corresponding spell is listed as a fast windup. The cue is part of the listed cast preparation; it does not secretly delay an otherwise defined attack.

### Common melee and guard

Every focus supports an emergency strike. Wand or staff butt strike deals 18 physical damage with 1.6 meter reach, a 0.8 second complete cycle, and 8 stamina cost. Light blades deal 28 with 1.8 meter reach, 0.8 second cycle, and 12 stamina. Heavy weapons deal 42 with 2.2 meter reach, 1.25 second cycle, and 20 stamina. Spears deal 32 with 2.8 meter reach, 1.05 second cycle, and 16 stamina. Unless an equipment record specifies a category, weapons use the light-blade profile; wands and staffs use the focus profile. Magical passive effects are added only when the chosen item explicitly permits them in its occupied slot.

Attacks use a swept strike volume matching their visible movement. They do not snap aim or track an enemy after the attack commits. One attack can damage its opponent once and may also contact props. Heavy attacks require 0.35 seconds windup, spears 0.25, light blades 0.20, and butt strikes 0.18; the rest of the cycle is recovery. Common melee is not a spell and does not trigger effects restricted to spell hits. Its damage can trigger eligible direct-hit effects within their shared budgets.

Guard costs 25 stamina upfront, lasts at most 0.8 seconds while held, and has a 3 second cooldown from release. A visible frontal 120 degree arc reduces weapon and projectile direct damage by 50 percent. The first 0.12 seconds is a perfect guard and reduces that damage by 80 percent, granting 5 mana once per guard when it successfully blocks. Guard does not stop ground fields, rear/flank attacks, boundary damage, or sound effects without physical projectiles. It reduces a spell's associated direct knockback by the same fraction but never reflects a projectile into an automatic hit. Normal guarding leaves a clearly punishable release window of 0.25 seconds.

Guard is an active directional defense applied before passive resistance and damage-reduction caps, so its temporary reduction is an explicit exception to the passive 45 percent ceiling. It never reaches complete immunity. A blade wizard's kit can alter its timing or follow-up only where specified; all other players retain the common action. Equip and swap actions take 0.35 seconds and cannot be used to cancel recovery. Changing the selected spell has no additional swap windup.

### Damage, shields, healing, and status

Damage schools express magic identity; damage channels determine resistance. Channels are physical, thermal, electrical, corrosive, and arcane. A spell's record states its channel, including any split. Most attacks have no headshot multiplier. Precision-tagged spells can earn a stated weak-point bonus with a maximum multiplier of 1.25. A head or focus strike cannot stack a second universal critical bonus.

Resolve an attack in this order: valid hit and guard angle; explicit precision multiplier; guard; channel resistance; other passive reductions; shield absorption; remaining health loss. Channel resistance caps at 35 percent and all passive reductions including resistance combine multiplicatively with a total cap of 45 percent. Negative resistance cannot fall below minus 15 percent. A split attack is calculated separately for each channel and rejoins for the original hit event, so it does not double on-hit triggers.

Maximum health caps at 450. Temporary and reserve shields share a 100 point cap. Gaining a larger shield replaces or tops up compatible shield capacity, rather than stacking invisible layers past the cap. Cast and triggered shields expire after at most 8 seconds. Explicit round-start reserve shields from equipment or augments persist until broken or the duel ends; they are issued once and never regenerate for free. Shield absorption spends the earliest-expiring capacity first, with remaining reserve and temporary capacity visible together. Direct healing from all sources caps at 35 per second per player and a maximum of 120 health restored across one duel, with a remaining-healing indicator in inspection. Lifesteal is direct damage only, caps at 10 percent, and is additionally limited to 20 health per second and the shared 120 duel budget. Healing never rewards self-damage or damage to props, summons, or training targets.

Hard control includes stun, root, silence, forced inability to act, and hostile displacement that prevents deliberate movement. Its single application caps at 0.75 seconds; silence caps at 0.6. After any hard control ends, the target receives 2 seconds of immunity to further hard control. Attempts during that period can still deal damage but cannot apply control or queue it for later. Continuous pulls use a visible movement force that a player can oppose and do not bypass this rule by repeatedly cancelling their input. Slows cap at 30 percent and only the strongest applies. Slow duration caps at 3 seconds and refreshed duration cannot hide its visual cue.

Wet increases reaction eligibility without adding a universal damage multiplier. Burn, venom, chill, brittle, charge, and marked are individual named statuses, described by their source. Damage-over-time effects from the same definition refresh duration and retain the strongest intensity; different definitions can coexist within the originating cast and tick budgets. Dispel removes the oldest removable hostile status, or the one named by its explicit selection rule. It does not remove boundary rules, enemy physical terrain, or the hard-control immunity protecting a target.

Reveal lasts at most 2 seconds and is shown to the revealed player. Invisibility lasts at most 1.5 seconds, ends on attack, cast, signature activation, or damage, and retains a nearby silhouette inside 4 meters. Invisibility does not suppress footsteps or neutral terrain reactions. Target-lock spells need sight at commitment and have break conditions; hidden players cannot be acquired through a UI outline. Neither sound nor reveal alone grants a spell permission to auto-hit through solid cover.

### Global modifier and trigger rules

Movement bonuses cap at plus 20 percent. A player can hold at most two dash charges; dash distance caps at 8 meters and teleport distance at 10. Permanent cooldown reduction caps at 25 percent, and no recharge may fall below 0.5 seconds. Mastery may improve one stated cast attribute by up to 15 percent or reduce its paid resource by up to 20 percent, never both on the same cast. Cost reduction from all sources has a 30 percent floor: at least 70 percent of the original cost must be paid, with subsequent refunds separately capped at 25 percent of that payment.

An effect may trigger once per 0.5 seconds and once per original target-hit event, whichever is less frequent. A beam's ticks do not each produce independent proc cascades. Secondary/proc damage cannot trigger on-hit, on-kill, resource-return, or another proc effect. One generation of secondary effects is permitted. A spell's own explicitly described reaction is part of that original cast and still consumes world budgets. Chain attacks jump at most three times, at most 6 meters per jump, and never hit the same opponent twice from one cast unless the spell explicitly describes a bounded channel.

A player can own three gameplay fields and two summons at once. Their maximum lifetime is 8 seconds. Creating a new one at the limit retires the oldest eligible owned field or summon, with a brief dissolution cue. Multiple non-interacting cosmetic ripples do not count because they have no gameplay effect. Neutral reaction fields created by a player count against that player's field limit. Ownership for bookkeeping does not grant immunity from their effects. If a catalogue record omits a limit, these global rules supply it; local text can impose stricter limits and cannot expand a global cap.

## 4 Physical world and reaction specification

### Representation and consistency

Gameplay physics uses visible, bounded objects and state volumes. It does not require a separate simulation for every visible droplet, ember, or dust particle. A water pool is a shallow collision-compatible field with connected wet cells; steam is a server-owned obscuration volume; ice is a temporary surface or destructible block; a wall is a validated cover mesh with durability. Rendered particles illustrate those authoritative objects and cannot change their collision or sight effects.

The arena surface is divided into 0.5 meter interaction cells near active effects. A cell stores water units 0 through 4, heat units 0 through 4, frost units 0 through 4, dust units 0 through 4, and material flags such as conductive, combustible, porous, or anchored. An operation modifies a bounded cell set based on a spell's declared footprint. Maximum active cell regions per duel is 128; repeated adjacent effects merge into contiguous representations rather than deleting meaningful states at random. Decorative material simulation remains local and cannot create damage, cover, sight, or sound information.

Humidity and wind are not random hidden multipliers. Any biome-specific gameplay modification appears in arena preview and in a compact in-combat environment panel. Cosmetic weather uses the same physical lighting rules on every graphics preset. A map with actual rainfall supplies a fixed, announced refill pulse and respects the same water-cell maximum as spells.

### Core reaction table

| Inputs | Condition and result | Combat purpose | Response |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Heat and water | Consume one heat and one water unit to form steam in their overlapping cells; 3 second base lifetime, 2 meter rise; no steam damage by itself | Break sight, disguise an approach, interrupt an aimed channel | Move, send a projectile through, or clear with wind |
| Frost and water | Two frost units consume one water unit and form ice for 5 seconds with 45 durability per local tile | Fast routes, slippery footing, brittle cover | Heat or a heavy impact breaks it |
| Heat and ice | Two heat units melt a tile into one water unit, consuming the heat; further heat may make steam | Convert cover into a sight blocker | Disengage before the next cast |
| Force and brittle ice | An impact of at least 20 direct damage breaks one struck tile and emits a 1 meter cone of shards for 10 physical damage, once per impact | Cover destruction and a limited secondary threat | Strike from outside the shard cone |
| Electricity and connected wet cells | Charge a connected patch for 0.6 seconds, maximum 6 meter propagation and 12 affected cells; first contact deals the source's declared reaction damage | Deny a route or punish a wet setup | Break wet connectivity, jump the short pulse, or ground it |
| Electricity and metal | Travel along one visible conductive object, maximum three branches and 6 meters each; object glows before release | Redirect attacks around a limited piece of cover | Leave its conductive contact area |
| Water and anchored conductor | Redirect one electrical branch into the grounded prop; the prop overloads after its stated capacity | Create a safe route for one committed electrical attack | Attack from a different angle or destroy the ground |
| Wind and steam or dust | A directional force above strength 1 translates the volume at up to 3 meters per second; strength 2 disperses its front 2 meter slice | Open a sightline or move concealment | Rebuild the screen or move with it |
| Water and burning material | One water unit removes one heat unit and suppresses that cell's burn for 2 seconds | Extinguish a route and deny reaction fuel | Reapply heat after the wet interruption |
| Heat and combustible growth | At least two heat units ignite temporary growth; it burns for 2 seconds, deals its declared damage, then consumes the growth | Punish plant cover and reshape an approach | Water or early retreat |
| Water and sand | Equal units create damp sand that reduces dust production for 3 seconds; no hard immobilization | Stabilize footing and defeat a sand screen | Dry it with bounded heat |
| Force and loose props | Apply a declared impulse subject to mass and speed caps; moving prop collisions cap at 25 physical damage per impact | Make mobile cover and attack angles | Dodge its telegraphed path or intercept it |
| Sound and solid cover | Sound is attenuated by material; an explicit sonic attack can shake fragile cover but cannot pass through arbitrary walls for full damage | Locate movement and pressure cover | Use thick materials or move after making noise |
| Light and prism props | A valid ray reflects along a previewed angle, with one reflection and 70 percent retained damage | Create geometry-based firing lines | Break the prism or leave the reflected lane |
| Shadow and bright light | Bright light reduces a shadow concealment volume's remaining lifetime by 1 second per second of exposure | Disrupt a specific concealment tool | Move the volume behind cover |
| Venom and water | A declared soluble venom effect dilutes to 50 percent damage and affects only its original bounded connected patch | Spread a small denial field with reduced lethality | Break the patch or wait its short lifetime |
| Gravity and projectiles | A visible field deflects eligible physical projectiles with a maximum 20 degree change; beams are not bent unless specified | Change predictable trajectories | Fire from another angle or use unaffected spell types |
| Arcane and active field | A declared dispel consumes one removable field layer; it does not delete permanent map geometry | Break a setup and create an opening | Stagger fields rather than layer them simultaneously |

Reaction strength values are part of the spell's world-interaction field. In the absence of a specific value, a quick single projectile deposits one local unit, a field deposits one unit per covered cell on creation, and a heavy direct projectile deposits two units at its impact cell and one in adjacent cells within 1 meter. Adding strength cannot exceed four units per cell. A material is affected only if its relevant flags permit the reaction. Heat on a painted stone wall does not make that wall combustible.

If multiple reactions are eligible in the same simulation step, process incoming direct impacts, heat-water/heat-ice/frost-water consumption, electricity connectivity, wind movement, then decay. Every reaction consumes its stated inputs before another reaction reads the cell. That sequence is fixed across clients and replay. Reactions cannot generate more energy than their source permits. A self-sustaining burn-water-steam-condense loop therefore runs out of purchased source strength.

Steam opacity is determined by cumulative path length through its volume. Two meters blocks target acquisition; the boundary remains visible as a contextual compass cue rather than a through-steam enemy marker. Steam does not disable audio, intercept projectiles, or apply wet to everyone inside by default. A spell may explicitly condense it back into bounded water, consuming the cloud. Graphics presets preserve the same silhouette suppression and volume edges.

### Terrain and impact rules

Permanent arena terrain is anchored and cannot be removed entirely. Frangible panels, prop covers, temporary walls, growth, ice, and declared terrain modules have durability and readable fracture stages. Damage removes validated subpieces; collision and VFX change in the same simulation update. No procedural destruction can create a hole into an inaccessible region, remove the central final duel floor, or drop a player through the map. A wall formed under a player raises them at most 0.5 meters or fails with a refunded placement; it never traps them inside collision.

Loose props have four mass classes: light 10, medium 30, heavy 80, and anchored. A normal force attack pushes light props up to 4 meters, medium up to 2, and heavy up to 0.5; anchored objects only shake or take durability damage. Velocity caps at 8 meters per second for damaging props. Collision damage is 5, 15, or 25 for light, medium, or heavy impacts above their threshold. Each prop damages a given player at most once per second and never triggers spell-hit lifesteal or cascading item damage. Player knockback distance caps at 4 meters per effect and respects control immunity.

Slippery ice reduces braking and increases lateral drift; it never randomly steals controls. Wet stone changes reaction eligibility and footstep sound, with no movement penalty by itself. Sticky growth slows within the global 30 percent limit. A declared traction item can reduce ice drift, but not remove every movement counter. Fall damage begins above a 3 meter drop, deals 10 physical damage per excess meter, and caps at 50; the generator offers safe descents. Outside-map falls return the player to the nearest valid platform with a 40 health match penalty and a 0.5 second visible recall. This penalty cannot activate item procs.

### Worked physical duel

A Water Pool fills a chokepoint. The opponent spends Fireball on its near edge, consuming local water and creating steam. A spellblade uses that steam to approach, but their footsteps remain audible and both players lose target acquisition through the same volume. A wind effect clears a narrow firing lane, exposing the approach rather than deleting the whole water setup. Frost then freezes the remaining pool into a slippery route. A player with traction boots can take that route more reliably, while their slower or less efficient equipment still imposes its specified cost. Every change comes from a kit spell, shared equipment effect, free augment, bounded source, and an opportunity for the opponent to respond.

## 5 Shared equipment and free augment progression

### Two separate decisions

Equipment is shared across all 36 wizards and purchased with match money. Spells belong exclusively to one wizard and are never bought or transferred. Augments are free, selected from a separate five-choice draft on scheduled rounds. Augments include general build effects, conditional combinations, wizard-specific enhancements, and major transformations of exclusive spells.

The structural reference is League of Legends Arena: rounds alternate combat with opportunities to obtain equipment and free game-changing augments. Arena describes Silver, Gold, and Prismatic augments offered at a common power level across players, including augment leveling and replacement. Confluence retains that principle with its own five-card draft, individual card rerolls, eligibility rules, and solo duels. [League of Legends Arena rules](https://support.riotgames.com/en-us/league-of-legends/gameplay/league-of-legends-arena-game-mode).

The transformation reference is Valorant Gauntlet Glitched: abilities can be upgraded and their behavior can change substantially. Confluence makes transformations explicit named augment choices with visible counterplay; it does not hide a random behavioral mutation inside an undisclosed roll. [Valorant Gauntlet Glitched rules](https://playvalorant.com/en-gb/news/game-updates/valorant-patch-notes-13-06/).

### Currency and equipment prices

Crowns are match-only money for equipment. Players receive 600 before the first equipment shop and 500 before each later scheduled or bracket equipment shop. Winning the previous combat round grants 100 additional Crowns. Draws, byes, and replay rounds grant no winner bonus. There is no interest, kill bounty, passive income effect, discount item, or premium purchase. Unspent money persists only until the match ends.

| Equipment tier | Price | Conclave unlock | Duel unlock | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 200 | Round 1 | Round 1 | Foundations and universally usable tools |
| 2 | 400 | Round 3 | Round 2 | Specialization and build direction |
| 3 | 600 | Round 6 | Round 4 | Strong conditional synergies |
| 4 | 800 | Round 9 | Round 6 | Major equipment effects with commitment |

The winner bonus gives modest extra purchase flexibility. Higher equipment tiers unlock for everyone by round, so wealth cannot unlock a stronger rarity stage early. Equipment never purchases augment tokens, free draft choices, rerolls, augment ranks, or another wizard’s spell. Starter plain focus, sidearm, and attire have no bonus and no resale value; they are issued outside the 120-item catalogue.

### Equipment shop

Open three equipment cards per shop. Each position has one independent free reroll. Buying any subset is legal within money, reserve space, and slot rules; a bought card remains empty until the next shop. A rerolled card cannot return the definition it replaced or any other current visible definition. No rolled item can cost more than the current balance. Equipment is drawn from unlocked affordable tiers, then uniformly among legal definitions in a tier. Owning a wizard is never an item eligibility condition.

Purchases recheck money and legality atomically. A remaining card that becomes unaffordable folds into an outside-budget placeholder rather than granting a new free draw. That card’s unused reroll can draw from the new affordable pool. If the pool is empty, show Save Crowns without consuming the reroll. Selling does not refill cards or restore rerolls.

Equipment slots are Main Focus, Sidearm, Armor, Clothing, Boots, Trinket A, Trinket B, and Consumable, with three reserve slots. Main Focus accepts any wand, staff, or weapon; Sidearm accepts a wand or weapon. A definition cannot occupy both. A nonempty Unique group cannot be equipped twice. All wizards can equip every item through their own casting grammar; conditional effects apply when their stated conditions are met, so affinities change synergy without class-locking the item. At most one equipment active and one consumable are enabled. Dormant actives are plainly labeled, and no inactive activation qualifies an eligibility condition requiring its active effect.

Equipment sells for 50 percent of its paid price. A used consumable sells for zero and disappears. A bought consumable has one use, spent on commitment; unused purchases persist to later rounds. Round restoration resets resources and persistent equipment cooldowns, not consumed purchases. Signatures and common melee are actions rather than equipment actives.

### Augment draft schedule

| Conclave round | Draft rarity | Free choices awarded | Candidates and rerolls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Silver | One | Five cards, one independent reroll each |
| 3 | Silver | One | Five cards, one independent reroll each |
| 5 | Gold | One | Five cards, one independent reroll each |
| 7 | Gold | One | Five cards, one independent reroll each |
| 9 | Prismatic | One | Five cards, one independent reroll each |
| 11 | Prismatic | One | Five cards, one independent reroll each |

Duel compresses those six drafts into rounds 1 through 6, with Silver in 1 and 2, Gold in 3 and 4, and Prismatic in 5 and 6. Bracket rounds and tied-round replays do not add new augment drafts. The rarity stage is shared across the lobby and does not depend on money or winning. Every chosen augment persists for the match unless explicitly replaced.

Equipment shopping and free spell selection happen first. Freeze the player’s equipment and equipped spells for the 30 second augment draft, ensuring its conditions refer to a definite loadout. Show five distinct eligible choices. At opening, include at least one current-wizard spell transformation when one is eligible and at least two universal or broadly conditional alternatives. The remaining two slots sample the full eligible pool. If no class transformation qualifies, replace that guarantee with an ordinary eligible choice and explain it in training, not as an error.

Each candidate has its own one-use free reroll. Reroll only replaces that candidate, excluding all definitions shown previously in this draft and all current cards. Selecting one card ends the entire draft. The player cannot take all five and cannot pay to buy another. Passing is legal but grants no banked token. Timing out keeps the existing build and chooses nothing.

There are six augment slots, maximum rank 2 per definition. A rank 2 offer consumes the same free choice and improves the owned augment in the same slot. New augment definitions match the current draft rarity; an owned augment’s rank 2 can appear at any draft stage whose rarity is at least its original rarity. An owned rank 2 never appears again. Replacing one owned augmentation with the chosen new definition is allowed and gives no money, extra reroll, or extra choice. Dependents of a removed parent become dormant. The player confirms that consequence before selection.

The server must maintain at least ten currently legal alternatives in each rarity for every wizard and loadout, enough for five opening cards and five distinct rerolls. Unconditional, mechanically useful fallback augments supply that floor. Eligibility conditions do not bypass draft rarity, unique-group conflicts, max ranks, or slot legality. The sampler avoids duplicate definitions; rank 2 is the existing definition’s upgrade, rather than a way to roll two simultaneous copies.

### Eligibility language

Eligibility is a structured predicate evaluated by the server and explained in plain language on the card. Conditions can combine ALL, ANY, NOT, thresholds, exact wizard identity, currently equipped or owned items, item tags, owned augment ranks, selected spell tags, round stage, and verified feats from previous completed duels. A player can inspect locked augments in the codex and see which prerequisites are missing.

The canonical JSON schema uses `all`, `any`, and `not` nodes. Leaves are `always`, `wizard`, `equipped_item`, `owned_item`, `equipped_tag` with tag and count, `augment` with id and rank, `spell`, `spell_tag` with tag and count, `round_at_least`, or `feat` with id and at_least. The `spell` leaf means the spell is in this wizard’s exclusive owned kit; `spell_tag` counts equipped spells only. `owned_item` may include reserve gear. `equipped_tag` counts equipment supplying that live tag, without including a disabled active. Every referenced ID must exist.

Extended bounded leaves support main-focus category, sidearm category, plain issued slots, slot tier, equipped-category counts with different Unique groups, remaining consumable charges, distinct spell tags, exact spell-tag counts, spell cooldown or windup thresholds, owned-augment tag counts, rank counts, and family counts. Their field schemas and examples are specified in the augment chapter. They use explicit enumerated IDs or tag sets rather than arbitrary code supplied by a client.

Spell-tag eligibility reads a structural profile made from the selected base kit, active wizard-specific transformations, and chosen shared equipment structural changes. A projectile transformed into a trap loses projectile and gains trap/field in that profile; school affinity remains. General shared augment effects are excluded from this eligibility profile. Shared-to-shared dependencies use owned-augment, rank, tag, or family leaves. After eligibility is resolved, the combat profile applies all active augment effects. This two-profile rule prevents a shared augment from qualifying itself with a tag it creates, or repeatedly disabling itself by removing its own required tag. Every shape conflict is shown before selection.

Example: ALL of WIZ-002; an equipped conductive focus; ANY of an owned rank 1 grounding augment or FEAT-020 completed; and NOT an equipped heavy-armor tag. This can offer a specific forge-circuit transformation while the same equipment remains usable by any other wizard. A second example requires two movement-tagged items, a rank 2 approach augment, two equipped projectile spells, and a previous duel with three dodge-followup hits. Deep conditions are intentional build goals, not random hidden gates.

Wizard, round, and completed-feat prerequisites are acquisition-only. Equipment, owned-augment, and equipped-spell conditions remain ongoing by default. If the next shop changes those requirements, the augment is dormant until they are restored. Dormant effects occupy their slot and retain rank but grant no statistics, triggers, or other augment qualification. Dependency evaluation is a topological walk; a dormant parent makes dependents dormant too. An augment cannot qualify itself, require a later rarity before first acquisition, or form a dependency cycle.

Reevaluate ongoing conditions after every finalized equipment/spell change and at duel start. Conditions never depend on the upcoming opponent’s hidden build, random future arena details, a purchase made after selecting the augment, unverified client claims, or lobby practice. A player cannot sell a required item after drafting and keep its gated augment active. No eligibility rule turns money into extra augmentation choices.

### Completed duel feat definitions

| Feat ID | Server verified condition in one completed duel |
| --- | --- |
| FEAT-001 | Deal at least 100 damage to the opponent |
| FEAT-002 | Land three different exclusive spells |
| FEAT-003 | Perform two successful perfect guards |
| FEAT-004 | Land three common melee attacks |
| FEAT-005 | Travel 60 meters of valid combat movement |
| FEAT-006 | Produce three distinct world reactions |
| FEAT-007 | Break two destructible covers |
| FEAT-008 | Land two hits within 1 second after a dodge |
| FEAT-009 | Land three direct hits from at least 15 meters |
| FEAT-010 | Survive below 25 percent health and win |
| FEAT-011 | Clear two hostile or neutral clouds |
| FEAT-012 | Deal at least 30 damage in each of two damage channels |
| FEAT-013 | Spend at least 120 mana through legal commitments |
| FEAT-014 | Complete five valid mastery casts |
| FEAT-015 | Destroy two hostile summons |
| FEAT-016 | Win without using a consumable |
| FEAT-017 | Absorb at least 60 damage with shields |
| FEAT-018 | Restore at least 40 health within the shared healing budget |
| FEAT-019 | Interrupt one committed hostile cast |
| FEAT-020 | Deal 30 damage through bounded conductivity reactions |
| FEAT-021 | Hit the opponent with one moved prop |
| FEAT-022 | Land three spell then weapon combinations within 1 second |
| FEAT-023 | Remove two hostile statuses |
| FEAT-024 | Return inside the closing boundary twice after taking its damage |

Feat leaves test the number of completed duels in this match meeting that definition. The normal threshold is one; a threshold of two requires two separate qualifying completed duels. Feats do not grant Crowns, slots, or extra choices. Training feats are visible practice records and do not satisfy competitive acquisition.

### Spell transformations and compatibility

Every wizard owns eight base spells and sixteen spell-specific augment choices: two authored transformations per spell. A transformation changes delivery, trajectory, payload, world reaction, recast behavior, summon behavior, or a combination with an explicit tradeoff. It does more than add a damage percentage. Its rank 2 deepens that same behavior. General augments add a further 288 choices that can connect equipment, movement, melee, reactions, mastery, and other augment chains.

Each transformation names the exact target spell and an exclusivity group. Mutually exclusive trajectory choices such as splitting, ricochet, returning, and portal routing cannot silently coexist. Compatible dimensions such as a shape change and a reaction change may combine only when their records permit it. The inspector shows the final spell form, all added costs and recovery, modified telegraph, effective caps, and which effect wins a conflict. Application order is base spell, chosen delivery/trajectory, reaction or payload modifiers, equipment modifiers, mastery, then global caps and proc budgets.

A transformation never acquires another wizard’s spell, copies their signature, or changes the selected wizard. Even if two kits use heat, their exclusive spells and transformation trees remain distinct. Shared gear can supply fuel, trajectory parameters, protection, or reaction hooks to either kit without erasing its casting identity.

## 6 Exclusive wizard content architecture

Each of the 36 wizards has a distinct casting grammar, eight unique base spells, one separate signature technique, and one passive. All eight spells are available only to that wizard from the start of the match. Equip six, defaulting to the first six, and freely swap within that eight-spell kit during preparation. Spells have mana/cooldowns but no Crown price. There are no shared universal spell slots, purchased spell books, cross-wizard spell theft, or random spells belonging to another character. Common guard, dodge, jump, sprint, and melee remain universal actions.

The catalogue contains 288 base spells grouped by owner rather than school. Wizard WIZ-001 owns SPL-001 through SPL-008; WIZ-036 owns SPL-281 through SPL-288. School labels describe physical affinity: Heat, Water, Frost, Storm, Earth, Metal, Growth, Light, Shadow, Sound, Gravity, Force, Spirit, Venom, Sand, and Arcane. A kit may mix affinities when its theme justifies them, allowing internal reactions such as heating its own water, or use the arena and shared gear to supply an absent material. Different wizards create combinations with the same neutral world rules.

Shared equipment is deliberately reduced to 120 definitions: 15 wands, 15 staffs, 20 mundane or magical weapons, 15 armor pieces, 15 magical clothing pieces, 15 boots, 15 trinkets, and 10 consumables. All wizard identities can equip them. The extra build complexity belongs to 864 free augments: 288 shared or conditionally shared definitions and 576 wizard spell transformations. Six equipped spells, one signature, one equipment active, and one consumable limit live controls even when the catalogue is large.

A spell keeps a recognizable core identity through transformations. If a ray becomes a prism trap, the changed form has an inspection icon, its own visible deployment, and an altered but recognizable school cue. A transformation must provide new timing or geometry and a corresponding opening for the opponent. It cannot keep the original name and animation while secretly becoming an unavoidable attack.

Catalogue numeric fields and prose effects are binding local specifications. Global rules fill omitted recovery, ownership, caps, physics strength, and status behavior. A local definition can impose a stricter restriction but cannot override a global ceiling. No catalogue surplus means every effect is simulated at once; each duel loads only the two players’ actual kits, equipped gear, active augments, and arena content.

## 7 Procedural arena generation

### Size and topology

Choose a diameter of 24, 32, 40, or 48 meters at round reveal. The size sequence is balanced across each consecutive four scheduled rounds: one of each diameter in a seeded order, without back-to-back extremes of 24 then 48 unless needed to preserve the four-round set. Actual usable area remains within 10 percent of its tier target. The boundary is an irregular but validated closed contour, not an invisible rectangular wall.

Generate a mirrored route skeleton with two spawn alcoves, a central final-duel floor, two side approaches, one longer firing lane, and at least two connecting crossover routes. Dress the skeleton asymmetrically with biome art while preserving equal route length, cover capacity, accessible resources, and elevation opportunity from each spawn. Gameplay props are mirrored or placed in symmetric pairs. Visual symmetry is optional; functional symmetry is mandatory in ranked presets.

The initial shortest path between spawns is 16 to 34 meters according to size, with neither spawn having a direct initial enemy sightline. A mobile melee build can reach useful central cover in 2.0 to 3.5 seconds without spending its signature. At least two approaches interrupt a ranged firing lane. The longest uninterrupted firing lane is 12 to 28 meters; no arena is exclusively corridors or open ground. Cover occupies 18 to 30 percent of usable floor area. No single cover piece blocks every approach.

Elevation differences are 0 through 3 meters in ordinary routes, with optional 4 meter vantage platforms that always have two access routes and a safe descent. Walkable ramps are at most 30 degrees; stairs and collision edges are standardized. Traversable gaps require only the common jump, while optional shortcut gaps may require a bought movement effect and never gate the only approach. Minimum route width is 2.5 meters; control fields cannot seal every connection between occupied regions.

### Generation pipeline

1. Pick size, biome, environment modifier, and recorded seed within the schedule constraints.
2. Assemble the route skeleton from validated modules, matching sockets and heights.
3. Add cover modules and props according to the biome's material and visibility budget.
4. Apply biome art and cosmetic variation without changing collision or gameplay state.
5. Place protected spawns, the central boundary destination, and standardized overhead lighting.
6. Validate reachability, route redundancy, sightline limits, cover ratios, mirrored distances, resource parity, movement footprints, and contraction paths.
7. Simulate representative field placements and destruction states to ensure no accessible region becomes sealed or unsupported.
8. If validation fails, retry up to eight seeds; then use a prevalidated fallback layout for that size and biome. Never release an invalid arena just to preserve randomness.

Random generation is server-authoritative and independent of player builds. It cannot deliberately generate a hostile map against a particular wizard or secretly prefer the current leader. Players adapt after the preview. Custom modes may select broader asymmetry, but their rules are labeled and their results are excluded from ranked ratings.

### Information and boundary

During shopping, display a rotatable top-down arena preview with diameter, spawn locations, cover and elevation shapes, material types, prop interaction icons, and the announced environment modifier. It does not show enemy live purchase decisions. The preview includes plain descriptions such as conductive rails, shallow water, combustible hedge, or prism surfaces, so players do not need to infer all material behavior from color.

Combat has no persistent enemy-tracking minimap. A compass and brief map overlay can show terrain and the approaching boundary. World interaction cues indicate charged, burning, brittle, wet, or displaced surfaces. Boundaries have visual, spatial-audio, and HUD cues whose intensity does not depend on cosmetic settings. Final contraction always leaves a usable central floor with opposing cover edges that degrade on schedule rather than producing an untouchable hiding pocket.

### Biomes and props

Twenty-four biomes change materials, atmosphere, module art, and one announced bounded environment rule. The rule applies symmetrically and never overrides global damage or control caps. Seventy-two modules form reusable topology, cover, elevation, and approach pieces. Forty-eight prop definitions give players destructible, movable, conductive, reflective, absorbent, flammable, acoustic, or reactive objects. Their complete specifications follow in the arena catalogue.

## 8 Interface and player flow

### Home, selection, and inspection

Home offers Play, Training, Codex, Collection, Replays, and Settings. The primary Play card shows Conclave, estimated duration, party restrictions, connection quality, and mode rules. A compact wizard selector supports filters for casting mechanic, preferred range, input complexity, and school identity. Hovering a wizard shows normal cast, mastery action, signature, passive, and a short playable preview. None of those filters declares a character stronger or easier to win with.

The lobby contains practice dummies and neutral props. Selecting a wizard loads its controls before matchmaking so players can test their chosen method. Input conflicts, missing microphone access for a selected voice mode, and unsupported custom bindings are resolved here; they cannot silently disable a kit in combat. If a microphone fails during a match, the equivalent rhythmic input mode becomes available instantly and keeps the same timing and telegraph.

### In-combat HUD

The HUD includes health and temporary shield, mana, stamina, selected spell and cooldown, six spell-slot states, signature state, one enabled equipment active, consumable, status icons, and round timer. Icons distinguish hard-control immunity, wet eligibility, damage-over-time, and remaining healing budget. Resource-affecting mastery feedback appears near the selected spell rather than covering the crosshair. A small directional sound indicator is available as an accessibility setting, with the same information latency and maximum resolution across supported inputs.

The crosshair communicates targetable geometry and spell spread, never enemy presence through concealment. Cooldowns display seconds and a charge count where relevant. The damage indicator reports direction only for damage the player actually received. There are no omniscient hitmarkers for firing into steam unless the shot causes an authoritative visible damage confirmation under the universal feedback rule.

### Shop and codex

Each equipment card shows name, tier price, effect, occupied slot, and its reroll indicator. Each of the five free augment cards shows rarity, rank, target spell, eligibility, transformation, and its own reroll indicator. Inspection expands exact numbers, caps, drawback, counterplay, and cause tags. A comparison view displays the proposed change and the item to replace. An inactive or capped component is labeled before purchase. The player may pin a desired catalogue definition as a reminder; pinning does not change offer odds.

The build panel displays occupied slots, reserve equipment, eight exclusive spells, six augmentation slots, active item choice, and final capped statistics. If raw bonuses exceed a cap, show both raw and effective values. The shop supports keyboard navigation, mouse, controller, text scaling, and a readable reduced-motion layout. A timeout commits only completed purchases and legal equipped choices; it never automatically buys a card.

### Results, death explanation, and replay

After a fight, show the decisive sequence: incoming attack, reaction contribution, guard/resistance/shield mitigation, status control, and final damage. For example: Fireball heated Water Pool; steam broke target acquisition; the opponent approached behind it; a heavy blade struck during guard recovery. Players can expand the sequence into numeric events or watch a short replay.

Round results display Resolve change, next baseline income, winner bonus, and remaining build. Match results show placement, actual competitive-rating change, wizard mastery challenges, cosmetic rewards, and saved discoveries. The UI explains ties and byes explicitly. Replay bookmarks can be shared as files or links only after player approval; the game never sends messages on the player's behalf.

## 9 Accessibility and mastery fairness

Voice casting recognizes an explicitly selected, finite vocabulary of invented syllables, phrase order, and cadence. It does not score accent conformity, loudness beyond a usable detection threshold, vocal pitch, or biological voice traits. A wizard can require accurate syllable distinction, but recognized confidence must exceed a calibrated reliable threshold before the game commits the cast. The local client shows what was heard before release for long incantations. Audio is processed locally by default; raw microphone audio is neither stored nor sent to opponents or match servers. The server receives only cast selection and timed commitment events, enforcing the same grammar windows as other inputs.

Every voice or rhythm grammar has an equivalent input route using timed directional or modifier presses with the same syllable count, cadence, exposure, commitment, and maximum reward. Recognition uncertainty gives no additional damage bonus. Input alternatives are tested for comparable error and completion time rather than assumed equal because they share a written description. Ranked matches permit all validated alternatives; an invalid alternative is fixed before shipping rather than declared inherently less legitimate.

Mouse gestures use forgiving normalization for scale and orientation where the rune definition permits it. The scoring tolerance rewards the intended recognizable shape, not perfect handwriting. A directional-key equivalent uses the same segment count and minimum draw duration. Continuous tracking classes retain their aim challenge, with settings for sensitivity, acceleration off by default, independent gesture sensitivity, hold/toggle options, and left-handed layouts.

Options include remappable controls, subtitles, dynamic subtitle size, color palettes that preserve material patterns, camera shake and motion blur reduction, field of view 80 through 110, separate voice/music/effects controls, mono audio compatibility, flash-intensity reduction, arachnid-free summon appearance alternatives with identical silhouettes, text-to-speech for menus, and scalable HUD. Camera effects can express an impact without compulsory disorientation. Performance and low-vision presets preserve concealment, enemy silhouettes, and threat cues.

A mastery reward is available through voluntary execution under pressure. High APM counts useful ordered inputs rather than repeated key spam. Failed mastery returns to the normal cast where the wizard record permits, or cancels with its explicit lockout. There are no recursive damage multipliers for a long input sequence. Every kit must pass tests for a competitive reliable baseline and a higher ceiling of control or resource use.

## 10 Training, AI, and discovery

The onboarding sequence teaches one aim spell, the common dodge, guard timing, melee reach, a water-fire steam reaction, one shop choice, and one short duel. It takes roughly 12 minutes and may be skipped or replayed. It does not force players through every catalogue entry. Subsequent wizard lessons teach that grammar's normal cast, optional mastery, signature opening, and counterplay in three short exercises.

The reaction garden contains resettable water, ice, metal, growth, sand, prisms, loose props, and walls. Players can examine state units, field lifetime, and event order in training. A build workbench equips any combination, shows caps and disabled triggers, and generates an explanation of the result using deterministic rules rather than unsupported claims that a build is optimal.

Bots have four competence settings. Novice telegraphs decisions and uses normal casts. Apprentice moves between cover and uses one reaction. Adept manages resources, guard, and simple multi-effect builds. Expert chooses among bounded plans using information acquired through actual sight and sound; it does not execute perfect gestures or parries every time. Reaction time has an explicit humanlike floor, and accuracy depends on projectile travel and movement. Training can separately enable a perfect mechanical demonstration bot whose noncompetitive purpose is labeled.

Discovery records a successfully executed named reaction or player-bookmarked combination. It stores involved catalogue IDs and a replay time, not a claim that the player invented the combination first. Players may name and save up to 100 local build plans. Exported plans include wizard, six spells, gear, augment ranks, input alternative, and game-version fingerprint. Import warns about unavailable or changed definitions and never purchases content automatically.

## 11 Competitive systems and social design

Conclave and Duel have separate hidden skill ratings and visible divisions. Conclave rating uses placement compared with expected placement in that lobby; tied placements use their mean occupied positions. Duel rating uses win, loss, or draw against the opponent's rating. Wizard-specific learning indicators are private coaching signals and never replace the player's match rating. New players have a provisional period and are preferentially matched with other new or similarly uncertain accounts when queue quality permits.

Matchmaking prioritizes region, connection, skill, uncertainty, and wait time. It never matches by spending, cosmetic ownership, engagement prediction, microphone type, or a hidden desire to create a win/loss streak. Minimum supported network conditions and queue estimates appear before entry. Ranked players can veto a region whose predicted connection exceeds the configured limit, accepting a longer wait.

The spectator system uses a minimum 15 second delay while a match remains active and restricts player-to-live-player messages. Eliminated players can inspect only public loadouts and delayed combat. Private custom hosts may choose a longer delay or approved live observers. Voice chat is optional in social/custom spaces; the spell microphone is a separate channel with a clear recording indicator. There is no required public voice chat during solo competitive duels.

Reporting categories cover cheating, abusive chat, offensive names, collusion, intentional disconnection, and technical issues. A user can mute text, social audio, and incoming invites separately without disabling spell input. Repeated deliberate timeout behavior may receive a competitive conduct response based on reviewable events, but a single long defensive fight is a legal strategy. Reconnect penalties distinguish an isolated connection failure from repeated abandonment.

Custom tournament tools include seeded brackets, rule fingerprints, observer slots, exported event logs, ready checks, pause requests between duels, and manual adjudication records. In-combat pauses require both players or an authorized tournament official; ordinary ranked matches cannot be paused unilaterally. Event organizers cannot covertly alter a player's offers or resources.

## 12 Art, sound, narrative, and content presentation

Wizards have recognizable hand silhouettes, focus posture, casting preparation, signature cue, and footstep treatment. Equipment appears on the body and in first person when practical; armor and clothing silhouettes remain within standardized hit volumes. A cosmetic may replace a material or ornament but cannot shrink a hitbox, silence movement, hide a spell windup, or make a common school unrecognizable.

School visual language combines color with shape and motion. Heat expands and sheds embers; Water flows in connected contours; Frost forms angular fractures; Storm branches with a visible origin; Earth has mass and crumbling edges; Metal has rigid aligned paths; Growth sprouts recognizable roots; Light has clean reflected rays; Shadow dims a bounded volume; Sound shows concentric pressure; Gravity bends a visible local field; Force uses impact direction; Spirit uses tethered translucent silhouettes; Venom has patterned droplets; Sand forms granular layers; Arcane uses geometric seams. Damage channels use inspection symbols independent of school colors.

Spatial audio communicates footing, preparation, release, travel, collision, and reaction. Occlusion attenuates sound according to declared material classes; steam obscures vision without pretending to be a solid acoustic wall. Mastery incantations heard by opponents are standardized in-game performances triggered by validated input events, rather than broadcasting private microphone audio. Musical casting kits use short authored motif fragments and mix priority rules so their inputs do not mask enemy attacks.

Narrative lives in wizard biographies, training dialogue, biome histories, collection captions, and optional short Conclave stories. It does not interrupt shop timers or obscure a competitive result. Wizard rivalries change lobby dialogue, with an option to reduce repetition. Every catalogue name and effect receives localization testing for short readable cards and consistent rules vocabulary.

Complete cosmetic categories are wizard outfits, hand/focus finishes, staff/wand/weapon skins, apparel appearances, idle animations, lobby emotes, recall effects, profile banners, titles, and codex illustrations. Opponent threat effects always retain the standard competitive silhouette and sound timing. A setting uses standard opponent cosmetic effects without removing purchased appearances in social spaces.

## 13 Account progression and business model

All 36 wizards and all gameplay catalogues are available from the beginning. Account progression awards cosmetic currency, titles, lore, and mastery challenge records. Challenges encourage varied play without requiring players to lose deliberately, purchase unusable items, or use a particular hardware input. There are no statistical account bonuses or permanent item improvements.

The complete commercial design is a single PC game purchase with optional directly priced cosmetics. A store shows the exact cosmetic preview, regional price, and included components. There are no paid loot boxes, purchasable match Crowns, paid rerolls, paid wizard unlocks, power battle passes, or energy timers. Cosmetic event rewards remain earnable through a permanent archive after the event's featured period, with its own transparent requirements.

Gameplay changes enter the competitive ruleset for all owners simultaneously. New cosmetics do not add item definitions. Saved builds and replay compatibility state the ruleset version. If additional gameplay content is introduced after the designed catalogue, it is an explicitly versioned expansion of this design rather than a hidden dependency for existing competitive builds.

## 14 Multiplayer and technical specification

The server owns health, mana, stamina, movement validation, casts, purchases, offers, field states, reactions, props, destruction, cooldowns, hit results, and pairing. Clients predict local movement and preparation for responsiveness, then reconcile to authoritative events. Cosmetic particle density is client-selected; gameplay volumes and collision are identical. A recorded seed plus authoritative event stream supports replays and bug reproduction.

The simulation target is 60 authoritative steps per second with 20 to 30 state snapshots per second selected by congestion. Rendering targets 120 frames per second at a competitive visual preset on the eventual published recommended hardware, with 60 as the minimum intended experience on validated supported hardware. Hardware requirements are set from measured production builds; this design does not invent a shipping GPU requirement. A worst-case duel budget contains twelve equipped exclusive spell slots across both players, six player-owned fields total, four summons total, 128 active interaction-cell regions, and 48 interactive props. Catalogue surplus never means every definition is simulated simultaneously.

Lag compensation uses a bounded history of player hit volumes with a maximum 150 millisecond rewind. Projectile travel, dynamic field state, and physical prop positions remain authoritative at impact; a client cannot rewind an old wall away after it was destroyed or target a player based on a speculative local steam gap. The server may adjust hit confirmation under documented network rules, but it never treats an unvalidated client damage report as final. High-ping conditions are shown and analyzed by region.

Cast grammar validation checks resource, selected spell, modifier cadence, minimum preparation, release order, cooldown, visibility prerequisites, and rate limits. The server cannot verify a human actually pronounced a syllable; voice events are validated as timed inputs, with the same commitment and benefit as the alternate route. Automation and cheating controls therefore rely on the general competitive enforcement model instead of pretending audio recognition proves human input.

Physics state is versioned and deterministic at the rule level. Exact art particles need not be deterministic. Build records, effects, and reactions have stable IDs. Replay includes ruleset hash, content definitions, arena seed, spawn assignment, and relevant event history; incompatible clients display a clear unsupported-version state rather than a misleading reconstruction. Server migrations preserve duel state or void a failed round for everyone in that server without granting manufactured wins.

Security design validates inventory transactions atomically, prevents duplicate purchase requests, rate-limits rerolls, verifies equip and Unique-group constraints, and rejects impossible movement or resource values. Server logs store rule events and account identifiers needed for support; raw voice audio is not part of ordinary telemetry. Anti-cheat implementation, privacy disclosure, platform compatibility, and legal/store requirements are reviewed against current requirements during production rather than assumed permanently settled here.

### Data model

Core entities are Player, WizardDefinition, ExclusiveSpellDefinition, SharedEquipmentDefinition, FreeAugmentDefinition, EligibilityPredicate, Loadout, ShopOffer, ArenaSeed, ModuleInstance, PropState, FieldState, CellState, CastEvent, DamageEvent, StatusEvent, DuelResult, MatchPlacement, and ReplayManifest. Definitions are immutable within a ruleset; instances reference stable IDs and track current resources, rank, duration, ownership, and disabled status. Effects expose trigger, condition, magnitude, channel, target filter, budget group, stacking rule, and permitted secondary events.

Offer RNG, arena RNG, cosmetic RNG, and bot RNG are separate streams. Rendering an extra particle cannot change a later shop offer. The content manifest lists every catalogue count and ID interval. Automated validation rejects dangling IDs, invalid tiers, unsupported slots, negative durations/costs, missing counterplay, and local exceptions that bypass global caps. Runtime transactions and reactions use the same validated definitions.

## 15 Balance and quality requirements

Balance goals are assessed over representative skill, input, build, and map-size groups. A wizard should retain a workable normal-cast baseline and show improvement through mastery. Aim accuracy should not decide every matchup; neither should one resource loop or one fixed build. Melee and ranged engagement plans both need counterplay across all legal size tiers.

Target indicators include wizard win rates centered near 50 percent in sufficiently sampled comparable groups, no common matchup routinely above 60 percent after accounting for player skill, and no individual item defining a mandatory purchase across most successful builds. These are investigation thresholds, not promises that every observed sample must fit a rigid number. Rare build combinations require qualitative replay inspection as well as aggregate statistics.

Shop review checks whether a losing player still buys meaningful tools, whether tier gating limits wealth advantage, whether no-offer states occur unexpectedly, and whether rerolls provide decisions without overwhelming the 35 second equipment timer and 30 second augmentation timer. Arena review checks approach safety, sightline limits, prop parity, contraction routes, and class performance by diameter. Voice and gesture review compares completion time and failure rates across validated alternatives and supported environments.

Required combat checks include all reaction pairs; hit-volume/animation agreement; common guard timing; simultaneous deaths; field ownership and retirement; connected-water electricity; neutral self-interactions; invisible-player cues; maximum shield/healing; rank stacking; proc budgets; summon limits; placement failure; boundary displacement; round restoration; consumable depletion; and purchase legality under concurrent requests.

Required procedural checks generate large seed batches for each size and biome, test mirrored distances and route redundancy, verify fallback layouts, and simulate destructive states. An authored counterplay scenario is required for every hard-control, concealment, summon, movement, high-damage, and multi-item transformation. The game cannot pass acceptance solely because catalogue entries load successfully.

The release gate requires the complete catalogue, complete training coverage by grammar family, stable full-match servers, functional accessibility alternatives, audited cosmetic readability, reconnect behavior, saved builds, codex, replays, ranked and custom rules, and the measured performance budget. The development plan can sequence these systems internally, but the intended final product includes them all.

## 16 Complete production content and handoff

Each wizard requires first-person hand and focus animation for normal preparation, mastery, release, recovery, signature, common melee, guard, impact, and recall; a third-person readable counterpart; biography; training exercises; selection portrait; input diagram; and localized audio cues. Shared rigs and animation layers are acceptable when they preserve that wizard's grammar and silhouette. Equipment requires inventory art, world/hand appearance where relevant, effect icons, card text, inspection text, and standardized activation cues.

Each spell requires hit geometry, cast phases, authoritative effect implementation, reaction strength, damage channel, resource values, counterplay scenario, telegraph/audio, accessibility rendering, training example, and codex entry. Each augmentation requires two ranks, trigger and stacking definitions, a capped-stat inspection result, and a combination test with its relevant tags. Every biome needs a complete validated layout library for all four diameters, collision/material flags, environment preview, sound profile, fallback seeds, and contraction destination.

The deliverable includes the narrative systems chapters, structured content catalogues, arena catalogue, and worked builds. JSON is the machine-readable catalogue; Markdown is the editable design text; the searchable HTML is the reading and review edition. A future implementation can import wizard ownership, eligibility predicates, stable IDs, and numeric fields while preserving the game's shared limits and counterplay requirements.


# Wizards, casting, and player mastery

Confluence has 36 fully playable wizards. Every wizard owns a different eight-spell kit from match start; six spells may be equipped, with the first six serving as the default loadout. Changing those six is free between duels. Spell definitions are exclusive to their wizard and cannot be bought, stolen, or obtained through another wizard's equipment.
